title: Jack-Tor

jokes.text: Rehearsal? We did a show last week.
jokes.setup: Tracy is being paged for rehearsal and Liz is chasing him down.
jokes.punchline: Tracy treats a weekly live show as if doing it once a week is excessive — revealing his total disconnect from professional norms.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly character-specific — Tracy's warped sense of work ethic is crystallized in one short line. The economy is excellent; no bloat. Strong opener that sets up the episode's Tracy conflict.

jokes.text: Next Friday is Damon Dash's birthday party. And the Friday after that there's an orgy over at Elizabeth Hasselbeck's.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Tracy he has to be in every show every Friday.
jokes.punchline: Tracy has mapped out his Friday conflicts — a celebrity birthday party and an orgy at a conservative TV personality's house — both delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The pairing is what makes it work: a plausible-ish celebrity event followed by the absurdist escalation of 'orgy at Elizabeth Hasselbeck's.' The specific choice of Hasselbeck — a conservative The View host — is a precise comedic selection. Highly quotable, strong originality, full character integration.

jokes.text: My acting style is like jazz. Jazz that you laugh at.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Tracy to read the cue cards; Tracy says he can't because he's an improviser.
jokes.punchline: He dignifies his improv with a jazz metaphor, then immediately undercuts it: 'Jazz that you laugh at' — admitting it's bad without realizing it.
jokes.explanation: This is top-tier 30 Rock economy. Tracy elevates himself with a pretentious metaphor, then accidentally demolishes the pretension in the same breath. The self-own without self-awareness is pure Tracy. Highly quotable and structurally tight — setup and punchline in two consecutive sentences.

jokes.text: It's a dance-pop techno hybrid called Muffin Top. I gave everybody copies at Christmas?
jokes.setup: Jenna tells Pete about her hit song.
jokes.punchline: The genre description is already absurd ('dance-pop techno hybrid'), but the casual revelation that she gave it as a Christmas gift — as if that's normal — sells it.
jokes.explanation: Good character work — Jenna's narcissism is established efficiently. The Christmas gift detail is a nice touch. Sets up the Muffin Top running gag.

jokes.text: Muffin Top is also number four in Belgium. / I said you could do it. / Why not?!
jokes.setup: Pete agrees to let Jenna perform Muffin Top. Jenna adds that it's #4 in Belgium.
jokes.punchline: Pete gives approval; Jenna — mishearing or not processing — responds with outrage 'Why not?!' before correcting to 'Oh. I mean, thank you.' Her brain is wired to fight for herself even when she's already won.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured reversal. Jenna's default mode is self-advocacy, so when she gets a 'yes' she processes it as a 'no' before catching herself. The structure (setup → apparent punchline → second punchline) is tight and the character logic is impeccable.

jokes.text: GE corporate video: 'For over a hundred years, GE has been imagining the future... today.'
jokes.setup: Jack presents a corporate video to the writing staff about product integration.
jokes.punchline: The slogan 'imagining the future... today' is meaningless corporate jargon played with total sincerity — a perfect parody of actual GE branding language.
jokes.explanation: Sharp corporate satire with meta resonance — this is literally NBC/GE's parent company being mocked on their own network. The slogan construction (future...today) is a real type of corporate gibberish.

jokes.text: 'Incorporate positive mentions -- or PosMens -- of GE products into your program.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains product integration to the writers.
jokes.punchline: The corporate coinage of 'PosMens' — casually introducing jargon as though it's already in common use — satirizes business-speak while making the cynicism of the request even more naked.
jokes.explanation: The invented acronym 'PosMens' is a great bit — corporate jargon that sounds plausible enough to be real. Strong character integration for Jack as the suit who naturalizes cynical practices.

jokes.text: Jack suggests writers integrate GE's 'direct-current drilling motors for an offshore or land-based project' into a sketch show.
jokes.setup: Jack explains how product integration could work on the show.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'direct-current drilling motors for an offshore or land-based project' in the context of a comedy sketch show is the joke — the complete mismatch of industrial product with entertainment.
jokes.explanation: The specificity elevates this above generic corporate satire. 'For an offshore or land-based project' is the killer detail — exhaustive technical language deployed in a comedy context. Jack's straight delivery makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Wow. This is diet Snapple? / I know, it tastes just like regular Snapple, doesn't it? / You should try Plum-A-Granate. It's amazing. / I only date guys who drink Snapple.
jokes.setup: Liz is mid-speech objecting to product integration.
jokes.punchline: The entire room instantly abandons their principled objection to become Snapple enthusiasts — a perfect illustration of product integration working in real time, on the show objecting to product integration.
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke for the episode and possibly the series. It's perfectly meta — the show satirizing product integration by doing product integration mid-rant against product integration. The escalating enthusiasm ('I only date guys who drink Snapple') takes it from clever to hilarious. Earns its 9 because the concept is original, structurally perfect, and practically invented a new mode of TV satire. Comparable to the calibration anchors in terms of cultural impact.

jokes.text: That's not fair. Josh gets a lot of fan mail for Gaybraham Lincoln.
jokes.setup: Jack dismisses the writers as artists saying they 'write skits mocking our presidents.'
jokes.punchline: Liz defends this with the specific example of 'Gaybraham Lincoln' — a recurring sketch character so absurd its name is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Gaybraham Lincoln' is a perfect comedy name — immediate, absurd, and it reveals the lowbrow nature of TGS in one compound word. Liz's earnest defense of it as high art is the character comedy layer. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: Did you guys know that Holland is the only country with a national dog? / I didn't know that. / Hmm. There's little facts under there.
jokes.setup: The tense product integration meeting has just broken up. Two writers have grabbed Snapple bottles.
jokes.punchline: They're reading the Snapple bottle caps — completely ignoring the serious workplace drama — while marveling at the trivia. The mundanity after the tension is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A callback that extends the Snapple bit beautifully — the room that was vehemently opposed to product integration is now leisurely enjoying Snapple facts. The understatement 'There's little facts under there' is perfectly delivered and makes the hypocrisy land without comment.

jokes.text: Hi. I'm Tracy Jordan. I'm black, NBC! Very proud, like peacocks, right, Janet?
jokes.setup: Liz insists Tracy can read because 'we shoot promos,' offering it as evidence.
jokes.punchline: The promo Tracy recites doesn't demonstrate reading — it's a word salad of disconnected NBC branding talking points delivered with manic energy, calling the floor manager 'Janet.'
jokes.explanation: Tracy's 'promo' is a perfectly absurd non sequitur that actually supports the illiteracy theory while seeming to refute it. The NBC peacock connection ('I'm black, NBC!') is a nice meta touch.

jokes.text: Hey, Tracy, I missed that last run-through. Could you run it once off cards for me? [Tracy refuses and leaves through a door] It says 'Emergency exit only.' He couldn't read that?
jokes.setup: Liz tries to test Tracy's reading ability without alerting him.
jokes.punchline: Tracy exits through a clearly labeled emergency exit door, triggering an alarm — his behavior accidentally confirming the illiteracy theory.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke — the test is planted, Tracy's action answers it through behavior rather than dialogue, and Liz's confused reaction lands the punchline. The visual gag does all the work.

jokes.text: What's really sad is that while she's in this fragile state, none of her friends are messing with her head. I think we should do something about that.
jokes.setup: Frank observes that Jenna is fragile and vulnerable since Tracy joined the show.
jokes.punchline: His 'concern' is immediately revealed as sadistic interest in messing with her — the non sequitur pivot from sympathy to scheming.
jokes.explanation: Clean inverted-logic joke. Sets up the B-plot efficiently. The fake concern into gleeful malice is a reliable sitcom construction, executed economically here.

jokes.text: My friend in accounting, Lando Calrissian...
jokes.setup: Frank is telling Jenna about a rumor from someone in accounting.
jokes.punchline: He name-drops 'Lando Calrissian' — a Star Wars character — as if this is a real NBC employee, delivered without any acknowledgment of absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan absurdism. Three words do all the work — no explanation, no wink, no callback. The commitment to the bit makes it funnier on rewatch. Frank as a writer-nerd using a Star Wars name for a fake mole is inspired character work.

jokes.text: It's like shooting fish in a barrel. / Yeah, if the fish have daddy issues.
jokes.setup: Frank and Toofer watch Jenna fall for their Lando Calrissian lie.
jokes.punchline: Toofer's addition of 'if the fish have daddy issues' upgrades the cliché with a psychologically specific burn on Jenna.
jokes.explanation: A great upgrade on an idiom — taking 'shooting fish in a barrel' and making it specific/psychological. The 'daddy issues' amendment adds a character layer to Jenna that will play out in her Jack-seduction subplot.

jokes.text: Tracy's 'movie' improv: 'Let's go rescue Karen or whatever. Is there a Cheryl? Then she could tell us where drugs are -- I mean gold -- then we got the car chase. I'm getting way too old for this!' / Was I supposed to say that then?
jokes.setup: Tracy is off-script during rehearsal.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's improvised 'action movie' stream-of-consciousness — mixing up names, accidentally revealing the 'gold' as 'drugs,' using the clichéd 'too old for this' — is a perfect parody of his unhinged film career.
jokes.explanation: Rich with comedic layering: the genre parody, the Freudian slip ('drugs — I mean gold'), and the meta confusion about cue cards. Tracy's 'Was I supposed to say that?' final beat is the perfect punctuation.

jokes.text: Look at the educational system in this country. We spend all this money in Iraq, but meanwhile, our inner-city graduation rates are lower than they are in the Sudan. / That doesn't sound right. / Maybe it was Sweden. Maybe it was teen pregnancy.
jokes.setup: Liz launches into a liberal speech about education inequality after suspecting Tracy is illiterate.
jokes.punchline: Her statistics collapse in real time — 'Sudan' becomes 'Sweden' becomes 'teen pregnancy' — revealing that she's performing progressive concern without actually knowing any facts.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. It targets liberal guilt and performative concern — Liz's speech is confident until challenged, then unravels completely. 'Maybe it was teen pregnancy' is a perfect non sequitur that's also a real social issue, which makes it funnier. Strong character integration: only Liz would do this.

jokes.text: I gotta read more.
jokes.setup: Liz's factual claims have just disintegrated.
jokes.punchline: Her self-assessment is 'I gotta read more' — a tone-deaf non-solution to her epistemic problem, delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. Four words, maximum irony — Liz's solution to not knowing facts about literacy is to... read more. The callback structure is tight and the self-unawareness is deeply in character.

jokes.text: I'm watching Friends right now. What happens with Ross and Rachel? No, no. Don't tell me. Seriously. What were you saying?
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz he's been studying comedy to understand what's funny.
jokes.punchline: His 'research' is Friends — and his attempt to maintain professional focus collapses immediately when he can't resist asking about the Ross/Rachel arc. The 'Seriously. What were you saying?' recovery is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy — Jack Donaghy, the most powerful man in the room, is completely undone by a sitcom cliffhanger. The structure (study → slip → recovery → no recovery) is perfectly controlled. The episode aired in 2006, when Friends was already in reruns, making Jack's 'research' even more absurd.

jokes.text: You're such a Monica!
jokes.setup: Liz tells Jack rehearsal is at 2:00, she'll fax changes by 9 a.m. — revealing her type-A organizational style.
jokes.punchline: Jack — who just admitted to watching Friends as comedy research — immediately deploys Friends character slang to call Liz uptight.
jokes.explanation: Clean callback that lands because it proves Jack immediately applied his Friends knowledge. The joke is also meta — it's a network exec using a competing network's show as his cultural reference point.

jokes.text: I have something the other actors don't. A secret weapon. / Oh, don't say your sexuality. / My sexuality! / Oh, God, Jenna, when has that ever worked?
jokes.setup: Jenna says she has a secret weapon to save her job.
jokes.punchline: Liz preemptively names it; Jenna had exactly that answer; Liz's 'when has that ever worked?' is met with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: The structure of Liz naming it before Jenna can say it is excellent — subverts the standard 'reveal' format. The character logic is solid: Jenna's sexuality IS always her answer.

jokes.text: Uh, when has it not worked? / It'll be a 45-minute wait. / Oh, will it? / Uh, yeah. Yeah, it will. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Jenna confidently asserts her sexuality always works.
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut to Jenna apparently trying her sexuality on someone who turns her down with 'it'll be a 45-minute wait' — she's been told to wait.
jokes.explanation: Effective cut-to that immediately deflates Jenna's confidence. The ambiguity of the scene (is she at a restaurant? at Jack's office?) adds to the comedy. The deflation is fast and economical.

jokes.text: Yeah, so now you just have to make yourself ten years younger and Asian.
jokes.setup: Jenna says she knows what Jack likes.
jokes.punchline: Liz specifies what Jack actually likes — 'ten years younger and Asian' — delivered as a simple, factual observation.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, specific, and slightly transgressive. The specificity ('ten years younger AND Asian' — both conditions required) makes it funnier than a vaguer version. Good character insight into Jack.

jokes.text: I don't know what to tell you. They're making me rehearse. I know Pat Benatar rarely performs live. Scalp the damn tickets.
jokes.setup: Tracy is on the phone, apparently handling a scheduling conflict.
jokes.punchline: Tracy is negotiating Pat Benatar concert tickets as a reason he can't rehearse — an utterly non sequitur commitment that he treats as an entirely valid work conflict.
jokes.explanation: Pat Benatar is a funny name-drop in context — specific enough to be absurd (not a current artist), and Tracy's brisk 'Scalp the damn tickets' resolution is perfect. One-sided phone calls are a reliable format and this one is well-executed.

jokes.text: Tray... Can you read? [long pause] Can I read?
jokes.setup: Liz works up the nerve to directly ask Tracy about his literacy.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's response — not 'of course I can!' or immediate denial, but a slow, deliberate 'Can I read?' — mimics the affected gravity of someone processing a serious accusation, which is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: The pause between the accusation and the echo is crucial. Tracy's mirroring of the question buys time dramatically while also being funny — it could mean he's offended OR he's performing the offense. The scene's cringe tension is well-built.

jokes.text: Did you ever see Hoop Dreams? It's like that.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to sensitively explain why illiteracy isn't Tracy's fault.
jokes.punchline: She reaches for 'Hoop Dreams' — a documentary about Black basketball players — as her cultural reference for Black poverty/inequality, which is an accidentally racist film choice that she deploys with total good faith.
jokes.explanation: The joke is on Liz — her attempt at empathy deploys a specific documentary that reduces Black experience to one film. It's a surgical strike on performative liberal allyship. Character-specific and well-earned.

jokes.text: I can't read, Liz Lemon! My shameful secret is out. Now you know why I'm always running into the ladies' bathroom. / I can't read! / I sign my name with an X! / I once tried to make mashed potatoes with laundry detergent!
jokes.setup: Tracy has just 'confessed' to Liz that he can't read.
jokes.punchline: Tracy escalates his confession into an absurdist list of unrelated calamities he attributes to illiteracy — ladies' bathroom, signing with an X, mashed potatoes with laundry detergent — each one more absurd and less logically connected.
jokes.explanation: This escalating confession is one of the episode's best jokes. The logic of 'illiteracy caused me to make mashed potatoes with laundry detergent' is completely absurd yet Tracy delivers it with total gravity. The escalation structure — from plausible (ladies' room) to plausible-ish (sign with an X) to completely nonsensical (laundry detergent) — is masterfully constructed. Pure Tracy and highly quotable.

jokes.text: I think I voted for Nader! Nader!
jokes.setup: Tracy's confession escalates through increasingly absurd illiteracy consequences.
jokes.punchline: Voting for Nader — and saying the name twice with horror — caps the escalation. A Black man accidentally voting for Nader (due to ballot illiteracy) is the political punchline that ties the absurdist list to reality.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. After laundry detergent (pure absurdism), 'Nader!' lands as a political gut-punch — the one horror that contextualizes all the others. The repeated 'Nader!' echoes the structure of the calibration anchor (Snip, snap, snip, snap). It's political, character-specific, escalatory, and has become a cultural reference point for the show. Justifies a 9+ — it's a punchline with real-world resonance, maximum economy, and peak Tracy character logic.

jokes.text: Damn, George Will just gets more and more conservative.
jokes.setup: Tracy is reading (or appears to be reading) at his desk.
jokes.punchline: The visual contradiction — Tracy, who just 'confessed' to illiteracy, casually critiquing a political columnist — begins to undermine the illiteracy con.
jokes.explanation: A quietly brilliant plant. Tracy is visibly literate — reading and opining on George Will — but nobody in the scene catches it. The audience sees it before Liz does, which adds a delightful dramatic irony layer.

jokes.text: The GE promo filming falls apart over dozens of takes — Jack can't remember 'product integration', asks for the line, is told not to give him the line, then asks again.
jokes.setup: Jack, the supremely confident GE executive, attempts to film a simple promo.
jokes.punchline: The extended sequence of failures — forgetting his line, arguing about line-giving protocol, then immediately asking for the line again — reduces the most powerful man in the building to a helpless amateur.
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe escalation — the humor compounds as each new take introduces a new failure mode. Jack's authority is utterly deflated while maintaining his verbal confidence, which is the core character comedy engine.

jokes.text: Line? / Sorry. My bad. / What's the first line? / Product integration! / Okay. Right, got it. I just need the first word. / Product! / What's the second word? / Integration.
jokes.setup: Jack is attempting to deliver his first line in the GE promo.
jokes.punchline: Jack needs the line broken down word by word — 'What's the second word?' — revealing his acting anxiety is so severe he's forgotten a two-word phrase he himself invented.
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best sustained gags. The escalating incompetence — needing the full line, then the first word, then the second word — is perfectly structured. The irony that 'product integration' is Jack's own concept makes it funnier. Then he immediately asks for the line again after being told not to ask for the line.

jokes.text: Why don't we go to lunch and we'll come back and maybe-- Let's all go have lunch.
jokes.setup: Jack's GE promo filming has been catastrophic.
jokes.punchline: The gentle suggestion to 'go to lunch' is the polite way of saying the shoot is a disaster — and the instant unanimous agreement ('Let's all go have lunch') confirms everyone needs an escape.
jokes.explanation: Functional button on the promo disaster sequence. The unanimous lunch agreement sells the scale of the failure without overstating it. Competent but not particularly memorable.

jokes.text: GE Promo. 126. / It's weird. What do I do with my arms? I've never thought about that before. Is it this? Or, if I may, this?
jokes.setup: Jack is now on take 126 of the GE promo.
jokes.punchline: Jack — a man who has presumably stood in rooms his whole life — has been so destabilized by acting that he no longer knows what to do with his arms. The take number (126) and 'if I may' formality are the kickers.
jokes.explanation: 'I've never thought about that before' is a great line — existential self-consciousness from one of TV's most self-possessed characters. 'If I may' formality while asking what to do with his arms is classic Jack incongruity.

jokes.text: 'New synergy' -- does that sound odd to anyone else? Does that sound like 'news energy'?
jokes.setup: Jack is reading from the promo script and second-guessing the language.
jokes.punchline: He mishears his own line as 'news energy' — a completely different and incoherent phrase — showing how far gone his performance anxiety has made him.
jokes.explanation: Good mid-sequence beat that adds to the promo disaster. The misheard-word problem is relatable and the specific mishearing ('news energy') is funny in its wrongness.

jokes.text: GE Promo. 129. It's called 'racial integration'-- No, that's not right, is it? It's called 'product intergort'-- 'intergortian'?
jokes.setup: Jack attempts to say 'product integration' on yet another take.
jokes.punchline: His brain produces 'racial integration' (the other, more loaded phrase) before mangling 'integration' into 'intergort' and 'intergortian' — completely invented non-words.
jokes.explanation: The 'racial integration' slip is the best single joke in the promo sequence — Jack's brain swapping in the more culturally loaded word reveals how deep his discomfort goes. 'Intergortian' as a fabricated word is also genuinely funny for its specificity.

jokes.text: Oh! Could we turn off the phones, please? / Oh, I'm sorr--ha! I'm sorry. That's me. Let me turn this thing off here. I think I just took a picture.
jokes.setup: Jack is mid-promo take when a phone goes off.
jokes.punchline: It's Jack's own phone, and his attempt to silence it accidentally takes a photo — a perfect small humiliation layered onto the larger disaster.
jokes.explanation: A reliable physical comedy beat — the person who complains about phones IS the phone person. 'I think I just took a picture' is a funny detail. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, everybody, there's a [bleep] pigeon. Shoo!
jokes.setup: The promo filming continues with compounding disasters.
jokes.punchline: A pigeon has apparently entered the studio. Jack — the GE executive — ends up shooing a pigeon mid-take, cursing in the process. The bleeping of the curse adds a comedic layer.
jokes.explanation: The pigeon is a great absurdist escalation in the disaster sequence — each new failure is more unexpected. Jack's formal 'I'm sorry, everybody' before the bleep is the character-specific touch.

jokes.text: GE Promo. 142. / ...in upward revenue stream dynamics. For all of us. / Cut. That's a wrap! Ha! That was fun, you guys. Didn't feel like five days, did it? / No. Nah, that wasn't bad. / Everybody have a good weekend. And...we'll be right back.
jokes.setup: After 142 takes and what's described as five days of shooting, the promo wraps.
jokes.punchline: Jack pretends it was breezy ('That was fun, you guys. Didn't feel like five days'), the crew politely agrees, and then Jack accidentally says 'we'll be right back' — a TV broadcast phrase, not a wrap phrase — suggesting he's finally absorbed ONE piece of TV language.
jokes.explanation: 'We'll be right back' as an accidental capper is brilliant — Jack has spent five days in TV-land and the only phrase that stuck is a commercial break cue. The plausible denial ('Didn't feel like five days') from someone who clearly suffered is perfectly Jack. Strong closer to the promo disaster arc.

jokes.text: I've summited Kilimanjaro. I've showered with Greta Van Susteren. I'm gonna do this, yeah.
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to psych himself up to do the live sketch.
jokes.punchline: His list of accomplishments climaxes at 'showered with Greta Van Susteren' — a specific, deliberately unglamorous celebrity that makes the list funny by subverting the expected escalation.
jokes.explanation: The specific choice of Greta Van Susteren — a Fox News legal commentator, not a glamorous person — is inspired. The joke works because 'showered with' is intimate language applied to someone nobody would expect, positioned as an achievement equivalent to summiting Kilimanjaro. Pure 30 Rock name-pick wit.

jokes.text: Are you guys gonna...correlate overseas earnings report dynamics? / Yes.
jokes.setup: Jack is pretending to take a call from his boss while actually stalling for Liz's benefit. Liz sees through the fake call.
jokes.punchline: Liz parodies corporate jargon with a random phrase; Jack's flat 'Yes' — refusing to break the pretense — is the deadpan punchline.
jokes.explanation: The single-word 'Yes' is the entire joke — Jack's commitment to the corporate persona even when called out is both funny and in-character. Quick and clean.

jokes.text: Jack's fake phone call to his 'boss' — performing a subordinate argument with empty authority-speak while Jenna watches.
jokes.setup: Jack is allegedly taking an important call from his corporate boss while Jenna observes.
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Jack is performing — the 'boss' lines are all hollow professional-speak ('Actions speak louder than words. Take care of it.') — and it's all for Jenna's benefit.
jokes.explanation: Good situational irony — Jack manufacturing a display of power for Jenna. Plays better on rewatch when we know the boss is fake.

jokes.text: How do you take your coffee, Ron? / I take it? Uh...I take it, uh, with the non-dairy creamer. / Mmm. Yeah. Non-dairy creamer. [seductive pause] Yum.
jokes.setup: Jenna has decided to seduce Jack's 'boss' to save her job.
jokes.punchline: Jenna is deploying maximum sexuality on a man whose answer about coffee creamer is 'non-dairy creamer' — and she treats this as deeply erotic. The 'Yum' is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from Jenna's seduction technique being completely indiscriminate — 'non-dairy creamer' is the least erotic possible answer, and she responds as if he said something devastatingly attractive. Her 'Yum' is perfectly committed.

jokes.text: The extended 'ahem/mmm/ahh' seduction noises from Jenna while presumably doing something weird with coffee
jokes.setup: Jenna is escalating her coffee-based seduction of Ron.
jokes.punchline: A series of escalating moans and exclamations ('Ahem. Mmm. Ahh. Oh, yeah. Eh-heh. Wow.') in what is clearly a public or semi-public setting — topped by someone shouting 'Quiet, please! Rehearsing!'
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that plays better on screen than on the page. The intrusion of the rehearsal call ('Quiet, please! Rehearsing!') is a funny environmental comment on the seduction scene.

jokes.text: I agree. It's the writing. It's not natural. / Uhh! Really? You think the problem is the writing? / Yeah. It's clunky.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to let Jack off the hook by saying he doesn't have to do the sketch.
jokes.punchline: Jack pivots immediately to blaming the writing — and when Liz is visibly stung, he doubles down: 'It's clunky.' His ego won't allow a graceful exit; he has to find someone else to blame.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jack character comedy — his pride forces him to blame the writers rather than admit inability. Liz's wounded 'Uhh! Really?' and Jack's oblivious 'It's clunky' is a beautifully calibrated exchange. The joke is entirely in the character logic.

jokes.text: No. You should definitely do it. It'll be hilarious. / Oh, well, that'd be a refreshing change of pace for the show, wouldn't it?
jokes.setup: After blaming the writing, Liz reverses course and insists Jack should do the sketch.
jokes.punchline: Jack's 'refreshing change of pace for the show' is a perfect counter-burn — using Liz's implication that the show isn't funny against her.
jokes.explanation: A good volley in the Liz/Jack sparring match. Jack's phrasing is precise — 'refreshing change of pace' is corporate-polite for 'your show isn't funny.' In-character and cutting.

jokes.text: No. Tracy took advantage of my white guilt, which is to be used only for good, like over-tipping and supporting Barack Obama.
jokes.setup: Pete accuses Liz of being racist for first thinking Tracy was illiterate, then thinking he was lazy.
jokes.punchline: Liz's defense is 'white guilt is to be used only for good' — and her examples of 'good' uses ('over-tipping and supporting Barack Obama') perfectly capture a certain type of politically well-intentioned but self-serving liberalism.
jokes.explanation: Tied with 'Nader!' as the episode's best joke. 'White guilt is to be used only for good, like over-tipping and supporting Barack Obama' is the kind of line that defines a character and a show simultaneously. The specificity ('over-tipping' as a guilty pleasure of liberal white people; 'Barack Obama' in 2006 as an aspirational political figure before he was president) gives it real cultural anchoring. This is quotable, character-defining, and a precise social observation. It's a line that would be equally funny in a comedy club. Justifies a 9+.

jokes.text: You hear this mess about sometimes Y being a vowel? What a world.
jokes.setup: Tracy has come in late saying he had to go to reading class.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's takeaway from reading class is existential outrage about Y being a vowel — treating a basic phonics rule as a scandal requiring philosophical processing.
jokes.explanation: 'What a world' as a response to the Y vowel rule is perfectly calibrated Tracy — it's genuinely confusing phonics treated as a revelation about the nature of reality. The economy is exceptional (14 words doing heavy character lifting). One of the episode's best one-liners.

jokes.text: The new TGS poster featuring Tracy has Tracy's name in giant letters while the other actors are nearly invisible — Tracy barely registers this and just says 'Yeah. It's good. I like it. Really?'
jokes.setup: Liz shows Tracy the new show posters. We can infer from context that Tracy's name/image dominates at the expense of others.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's bored approval — after his colleagues are apparently horrified — suggests he finds this perfectly normal.
jokes.explanation: Visual gag that requires seeing the poster to fully land, but Tracy's complete nonchalance about what is apparently an outrage to others is in-character and functional.

jokes.text: I'll be leaving early today.
jokes.setup: Tracy came in late for reading class, barely stayed, showed up for the poster reveal.
jokes.punchline: His immediate 'I'll be leaving early today' — after just arriving — is the perfect punctuation to his noncommittal work ethic.
jokes.explanation: One sentence, all character. Tracy came in late and is already leaving early. The deadpan economy earns it a higher score than the underlying concept merits.

jokes.text: /Jenna and Ghostface Killah to the stage, please, for Muffin Top.
jokes.setup: Jenna's Muffin Top rehearsal needs are escalating.
jokes.punchline: The paging system now includes Ghostface Killah — a Wu-Tang Clan rapper — as a Muffin Top collaborator, announced matter-of-factly.
jokes.explanation: The escalating Muffin Top announcements are a running gag — each page adds a more absurd collaborator. Ghostface Killah is a funny choice because of the incongruity with Jenna and the song genre. The gag is set up for a bigger payoff later.

jokes.text: That's quite a commitment to such terrible writing.
jokes.setup: Jack calls Liz at 3 a.m., apparently having been practicing his lines all night.
jokes.punchline: Liz's response — acknowledging both his dedication AND that the writing is bad — is a backhanded compliment that somehow makes both of them look worse.
jokes.explanation: A callback to Jack's 'clunky writing' complaint — Liz now conceding the writing IS bad while pointing out Jack is practicing it obsessively anyway. The irony is clean.

jokes.text: I don't get it. It's not the fear. I thrive on fear. / You're looking out a fake window right now, by the way. / I bow-hunt polar bear. I once drove a rental car into the Hudson just to practice escaping.
jokes.setup: Jack is at the studio at 3 a.m., trying to understand why he can't act.
jokes.punchline: As Jack lists his fearlessness credentials, Liz notes he's staring out a fake window — undermining his bravado while he's mid-brag. 'Bow-hunt polar bear' and 'drove a rental car into the Hudson to practice escaping' escalate the absurdity of his courage resume.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. Three distinct funny elements working together: (1) Liz's flat 'fake window' interjection deflating Jack's self-mythology in real time; (2) 'bow-hunt polar bear' as a specific, escalating bravado claim; (3) 'drove a rental car into the Hudson to practice escaping' — the 'rental' detail makes it funnier (frugal even in danger) and the 'practice' adds bureaucratic intentionality to a death-defying act. All three would be funny individually. Together they're exceptional.

jokes.text: You're looking out a fake window right now, by the way. / I bow-hunt polar bear. / I once drove a rental car into the Hudson just to practice escaping.
jokes.setup: Jack is insisting his inability to act isn't fear — he's a man of extraordinary physical courage.
jokes.punchline: Three escalating proof-points of Jack's toughness: fake window (contextual aside), bow-hunting polar bears (extreme sport), and deliberately driving into a river for practice (pathological preparedness).
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character comedy. Three revelations in quick succession paint a portrait of Jack as someone who has prepared for every conceivable physical emergency except performing on TV. 'I once drove a rental car into the Hudson just to practice escaping' is a perfect Jack Donaghy sentence — the 'rental' car detail is inspired (of course he'd wreck a rental, not his own).

jokes.text: Oh, God, the room is spinning. What do you want from me? I'm one of your actors. I'm freaking out. Talk me down.
jokes.setup: Jack, who has lectured everyone about strength and leadership, is having a stage-fright meltdown.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm one of your actors' — Jack placing himself on the same level as Josh, who eats club sandwiches with toothpicks in them — is the self-abasement that makes this funny.
jokes.explanation: Jack's complete abandonment of his authority persona is the joke. 'Talk me down' from Jack Donaghy is inherently funny.

jokes.text: Josh can do this, and earlier today he ate a club sandwich with the toothpicks still in it. Jenna can do this, and she was once engaged to David Blaine.
jokes.setup: Liz is giving Jack a pep talk, arguing that if less-capable people can act, so can he.
jokes.punchline: Her evidence for Josh's incompetence is 'he ate a club sandwich with the toothpicks still in it' — an absurdly specific detail. For Jenna, 'engaged to David Blaine' — implying Jenna's judgment is so poor she got engaged to a magician known for bizarre endurance stunts.
jokes.explanation: Both specifics are excellent: 'toothpicks still in it' as proof of Josh's stupidity is the kind of hyper-specific detail that 30 Rock excels at. 'Engaged to David Blaine' is perfect for Jenna — implying she's both gullible (he's a showman) and has terrible taste. These aren't random name-drops; they're precisely chosen for maximum comedic effect.

jokes.text: If you were any other woman on earth... I would be turned on right now.
jokes.setup: Liz has just delivered a tough, manly pep talk that ends with 'be a man and get it done.'
jokes.punchline: Jack's response acknowledges her speech was objectively hot — but the Liz exception ('any other woman on earth') makes it a non-compliment compliment.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes and one of the defining Jack/Liz dynamic jokes in the series. It perfectly encapsulates their relationship: mutual respect mixed with Jack's dismissal of Liz as a romantic prospect. The structure is elegant — the compliment is genuine until the qualifier makes it an insult. It's also deeply quotable and became a touchstone for the Jack-Liz dynamic throughout the series. Justified 8.7/9.0.

jokes.text: This stays between us, right, Lemon? / [long pause] / Lemon?
jokes.setup: Jack has just had an extremely vulnerable moment with Liz.
jokes.punchline: Liz's silence — she doesn't answer — is itself the answer. The second 'Lemon?' confirms she's not going to commit. The audience knows she's going to watch the show.
jokes.explanation: The pause-as-answer is well-executed. The repeat of 'Lemon?' after receiving no response is a perfectly timed comedic beat — Jack knows she's not going to commit, and so does the audience. Non-verbal comedy that works in a transcript because the second 'Lemon?' confirms the silence was meaningful.

jokes.text: I hooked up with his boss. / Who, Ron? / Mm-hmm. / That guy's an extra on the show. / No. He said he was Jack's boss. / No. In the sketch. He doesn't even have a line.
jokes.setup: Jenna triumphantly reports that she secured her job by seducing Jack's boss.
jokes.punchline: The 'boss' was a background extra in the product integration sketch — not a real GE executive at all. Jenna seduced a man who doesn't even have lines.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed reveal that pays off two earlier plants: the fake phone call (where Ron played Jack's boss for Jenna's benefit) and Jenna's 'non-dairy creamer' seduction. The escalating revelation ('that guy's an extra' → 'he doesn't even have a line') is well-structured and the callback works perfectly.

jokes.text: What is the point of belonging to the Extras Guild if I cannot get health coverage for my foot, hmm?
jokes.setup: Ron, the extra Jenna seduced, is now revealed to be a real person with real concerns.
jokes.punchline: His grievance is specifically about Extras Guild health coverage for his foot — a hyper-specific complaint that deflates the romantic subplot while making Ron a full (absurd) character.
jokes.explanation: 'My foot' as the specific uninsured body part is a great choice — mundane and absurd simultaneously. The Extras Guild complaint comes from nowhere and lands with perfect specificity. One of the better peripheral character jokes.

jokes.text: I am gonna get back at them...using my sexuality. / Do you have any left?
jokes.setup: Jenna announces she'll use her sexuality to get revenge on Frank and Toofer.
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'Do you have any left?' — implying Jenna has depleted her sexuality by seducing Ron the Extra — is a brutal callback delivered flatly.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly calibrated burn — 'Do you have any left?' treats sexuality as a finite resource that Jenna has now wasted. The economy is excellent (six words). Liz's deadpan delivery of this is crucial; it's not cruel, just observational.

jokes.text: /Jenna, Ghostface Killah, and Yo-Yo Ma to the stage, please, for Muffin Top.
jokes.setup: The Muffin Top page escalation continues.
jokes.punchline: Yo-Yo Ma — the world's most celebrated classical cellist — has been added to the Muffin Top lineup alongside Ghostface Killah. The collision of genres and cultural prestige levels is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The running gag peaks here — Ghostface Killah was already absurd, but Yo-Yo Ma makes the collaboration list so absurd it becomes a statement about the show's anything-goes comedy philosophy. The three-way collision of a dancepop-nobody, a Wu-Tang rapper, and a classical cellist is inspired.

jokes.text: Where the hot lesbians at, Lemon? / I knew it! You can read!
jokes.setup: Tracy finds Liz. His opening line reveals literacy.
jokes.punchline: Tracy asks about 'hot lesbians' — presumably from a script or cue card — and Liz catches him reading out loud without realizing it.
jokes.explanation: The illiteracy plot resolves with Tracy accidentally reading out loud — a perfect situational reveal. 'Where the hot lesbians at?' is also funny on its own merits as a non sequitur opener. The catch is structurally satisfying.

jokes.text: I even have a column in Ebony called Musings!
jokes.setup: Tracy confirms he's literate.
jokes.punchline: Not only can Tracy read, he has a regular column in Ebony magazine called 'Musings' — an absurd escalation that suggests he's actually quite literate and intellectual when he wants to be.
jokes.explanation: 'Musings' in Ebony is a perfect joke — the column title is both pretentious and delightful, and it reveals that Tracy's chosen vehicle for literary expression is about as far from his on-screen persona as possible. The confidence with which he delivers it makes it land harder.

jokes.text: That's the subtle racism of lowered expectations. Bing Crosby said that. / No, Bill Cosby said that. / That's racist. / Look, we can all agree Liz is generally pretty racist.
jokes.setup: Tracy accuses Liz of 'the subtle racism of lowered expectations' but attributes the phrase to Bing Crosby.
jokes.punchline: Liz corrects him: it's Bill Cosby. Tracy's response: 'That's racist' — presumably because Liz knows which Black person said something. Pete's 'we can all agree Liz is generally pretty racist' is the final button.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly layered joke. Tracy uses the phrase slightly wrong (wrong Crosby/Cosby); Liz corrects him demonstrating knowledge of racial attribution; Tracy calls THAT racist; and Pete delivers the episode's thematic button with 'we can all agree Liz is generally pretty racist.' Three distinct comedic beats in four lines, each escalating. The Bing/Bill Crosby/Cosby confusion is inspired wordplay.

jokes.text: Look, we can all agree Liz is generally pretty racist.
jokes.setup: The Bing/Bill Cosby quote debate has devolved into an accusation spiral.
jokes.punchline: Pete cuts through the argument with a breezy consensus statement as if Liz's racism is a known fact everyone has accepted — his casualness is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Strong button on the racism theme. The deadpan consensus framing — 'we can all agree' — treats Liz's racism as established fact in a company-wide sense, which is both a good joke and a callback to Pete's earlier accusation.

jokes.text: You know, I once shot a whole movie without ever getting out of my car? / Yeah, I paid to see that. That was supposed to be a western.
jokes.setup: Tracy complains that his job is hard and he just wants to do what he wants to do.
jokes.punchline: He cites a movie he made without leaving his car as a creative achievement; Liz — who apparently saw it — confirms it was supposed to be a western, making the car non sequitur even more absurd.
jokes.explanation: The two-person structure here is what elevates it: Tracy's absurd claim is immediately confirmed AND extended by Liz — 'I paid to see that' shows she willingly attended. The 'western' detail recontextualizes the car-acting as even more inexplicable. This is a perfect 30 Rock two-line joke.

jokes.text: Yeah, I paid to see that. That was supposed to be a western.
jokes.setup: Tracy cites his car-bound movie as a legitimate work achievement.
jokes.punchline: Pete confirms he paid to see it — and the kicker is that it was supposed to be a western, implying the film's setting (a car) was wholly incompatible with its genre.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback/button. 'That was supposed to be a western' is a devastating addition — it implies a car-bound western, which is a perfect absurdist image. Pete's flat delivery makes it funnier.

jokes.text: When Gaybraham Lincoln gets hit in the crotch, can I go cross-eyed? / Oh, yes, do that. That's hilarious!
jokes.setup: Liz has just given Tracy a serious speech about professionalism and reading lines as written.
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately negotiates a physical comedy caveat for Gaybraham Lincoln (the sketch name-dropped earlier). Liz — who was just being very serious — cracks immediately and endorses it.
jokes.explanation: A callback that also deflates Liz's just-delivered professionalism speech — she crumbles the moment Tracy offers something genuinely funny. Her immediate 'That's hilarious!' reveals that beneath her authority-figure pose, she's still just a comedy writer who loves a stupid bit.

jokes.text: The standards lady is saying that my moaning in Muffin Top is too graphic. Which of these is less offensive? Ahh! Ahh! Ahhh! Or...Ooh-hunh! Unh-hunh! Ohhh!
jokes.setup: Jenna approaches Pete with a standards complaint about her Muffin Top moaning.
jokes.punchline: Her 'which is less offensive' question is rendered moot because both options are clearly equally graphic — she's asking Pete to arbitrate between two identical levels of sexual noise.
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe comedy — Pete is trapped into adjudicating an impossible standards question. Jenna's obliviousness to the equivalence of both options is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Hello, Ron.
jokes.setup: Jenna encounters Ron (the extra she seduced) in the hallway.
jokes.punchline: Her breezy 'Hello, Ron' — treating the man she accidentally slept with believing him to be a GE executive as a casual acquaintance — is the perfect callback delivered in two words.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — two words carrying the full weight of the Ron subplot. Jenna's breezy normalization of what happened is exactly right for the character.

jokes.text: Lemon, these pages are blank. / Oh. / Never mind. / Withdrawn. / And, remember, don't look into the camera!
jokes.setup: Liz hands Jack 'new pages' with all the changes to his sketch right before showtime.
jokes.punchline: The pages are blank — Liz was trying to gaslight Jack into thinking changes had been made so he'd be confused enough to just perform naturally. 'Withdrawn' is a perfect word choice, and 'don't look into the camera' as the parting shot is the button.
jokes.explanation: Sharp and well-structured. The blank pages reveal is a great twist — Liz's solution to Jack's performance anxiety is to trick him with nothing. 'Withdrawn' (a legal/formal word choice) perfectly characterizes Jack's response, and the departing 'don't look into the camera!' is a perfect button that calls back to all his earlier camera-looking problems.

jokes.text: So we had to make some changes. Tracy is now in it, so we had to change some cues. Also, the opening VT is cut, so you just go right out. Oh, and you all say the last line together. / Wow. So uh... [Liz leaves] / Lemon, these pages are blank. / Oh. / Never mind. / Withdrawn.
jokes.setup: Liz gives Jack 'new pages' with last-minute changes for the sketch.
jokes.punchline: The pages are blank — Liz has handed him nothing. Her casual 'Oh. / Never mind. / Withdrawn.' suggests this was possibly intentional, definitely negligent, and perfectly illustrates her management style.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured gag. The elaborate setup of 'new pages' with specific changes makes the blank reveal funnier. Liz's three-part response — 'Oh. / Never mind. / Withdrawn.' — is a lawyer-register word ('Withdrawn') deployed in a casual context, which is a perfect 30 Rock flourish. Jack's 'And, remember, don't look into the camera!' as she leaves is the cherry on top.

jokes.text: I have this fantasy of sneaking up to the roof of 30 Rock, and we make love while looking out at the city -- / Okay, let me guess. You figured out Frank and I lied to you, so to get even, you're trying to get me naked on the roof and leave me there.
jokes.setup: Jenna approaches Toofer with a 'confession' about her rooftop fantasy.
jokes.punchline: Toofer preemptively names the entire revenge scheme — Jenna planned to leave him naked on the roof — before she can deliver the punchline, defusing her revenge and revealing how well these writers know each other's tricks.
jokes.explanation: A subversion of the expected structure — normally the seduction attempt would play out before being caught. Toofer's pre-emptive full diagnosis of the revenge plot ('get me naked on the roof and leave me there') is funnier than the gag itself would have been. The 'naked on the roof' specificity is a nice detail.

jokes.text: I have this fantasy of sneaking up to the roof of 30 Rock, and we make love while looking out at the city-- / Okay, let me guess. You figured out Frank and I lied to you, so to get even, you're trying to get me naked on the roof and leave me there.
jokes.setup: Jenna approaches Toofer seductively with what sounds like a romantic proposition.
jokes.punchline: Toofer immediately sees through the transparent revenge plot — and his specific description ('get me naked on the roof and leave me there') reveals this is such an obvious play that it has an established name/form.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal. The seduction speech has a classic rom-com cadence until Toofer cuts it off with complete knowledge of the plan. The 'leave me there' detail implies this scheme has specific physical parameters that Toofer is entirely familiar with.

jokes.text: But we're cool, right, Mr. Donaghy? / No, you're all fired.
jokes.setup: After the sketch, Josh addresses Jack hoping the awkwardness is over.
jokes.punchline: Jack's flat 'No, you're all fired' — whether real or a power flex — is the most Jack possible response: no processing, no forgiveness, just immediate decisive action.
jokes.explanation: The humor is entirely in Jack's delivery and character logic — a normal person would say 'we're fine' or even ignore it. Jack says 'No, you're all fired.' The ambiguity (is he serious?) is appropriately unresolved.

jokes.text: Hey, good job the other night. / Oh, you mean on the show? Thanks. / What were you watching? / Nothing. Uh...Bloomberg. / Hmm. / Aha! / Don't be cute, Lemon. You're too old for that.
jokes.setup: Liz has clearly watched Jack on the show (violating the 'it stays between us' agreement).
jokes.punchline: Jack's cover story 'Bloomberg' is immediately transparent; Liz's 'Aha!' catches him; Jack's 'Don't be cute, Lemon. You're too old for that' is a pure deflection-as-insult.
jokes.explanation: A clean resolution to the 'this stays between us' promise — Liz watched, Jack knows she watched, neither will acknowledge it directly. 'You're too old for that' as Jack's deflection from embarrassment is a perfectly calibrated burn.

jokes.text: Hey, good job the other night. / Oh, you mean on the show? Thanks. / What were you watching? / Nothing. Uh... Bloomberg.
jokes.setup: Jack compliments Liz on her 'good job the other night.'
jokes.punchline: When Liz asks what he was watching, Jack claims 'Bloomberg' — but has clearly been watching TGS (and her). His cover story is a business news channel, perfectly in character.
jokes.explanation: Good character moment — Jack watching TGS and claiming Bloomberg is quintessential Jack deflection. The 'Nothing. Uh...' hesitation before Bloomberg is a nice acting beat that makes the lie transparent.

jokes.text: Aha! / Don't be cute, Lemon. You're too old for that.
jokes.setup: Liz catches Jack in his Bloomberg lie and triumphantly calls it out.
jokes.punchline: Jack's response to being caught — 'Don't be cute, Lemon. You're too old for that' — is both a dismissal and an insult, refusing to concede the point by going on offense.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack deflection. He's been caught watching TGS and his response is to attack Liz's age — a perfect character move. 'You're too old for that' has a nice sting that makes it more than a simple put-down.

jokes.text: Good God! Lemon! [Liz opens the door] Mr. Donaghy, open up! Please?
jokes.setup: Jack sees Liz in the corridor after their conversation.
jokes.punchline: The sudden commotion — Jack's 'Good God! Lemon!' followed by Liz banging on a door — implies Jack has locked himself in a room in response to Liz 'being cute,' treating a mild social awkwardness as an emergency.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy beat that punctuates the scene. Jack's 'Good God!' is his signature register for being caught off-guard. Functional and energetic but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: The Muffin Top performance plays out onstage; the lyrics ('whole grain, low-fat,' 'I run a tidy bakery,' 'The boys all want my cake for free') continue after the show has gone off the air.
jokes.setup: Muffin Top has been teased all episode as Jenna's crowning achievement.
jokes.punchline: The song continues for an extended period — and Jenna keeps performing, oblivious that they went off the air two minutes ago. The song itself (which is about a muffin top while being about... other muffin tops) lands as cringe comedy.
jokes.explanation: The episode-long Muffin Top tease pays off with the song being genuinely absurd — the lyrics walk a perfect line between earnest pop and unintentional self-parody. The kicker (the show went off air) perfectly encapsulates Jenna's delusion.

jokes.text: Does she know we went off the air two minutes ago? / No, she does not. / Smart move.
jokes.setup: Jenna is still performing Muffin Top.
jokes.punchline: Pete's 'Smart move' — endorsing the decision NOT to tell Jenna the show has ended — is the final joke of the episode. It suggests everyone has learned that with Jenna, sometimes you just let the chaos play out.
jokes.explanation: A perfect button for the episode. 'Smart move' as an endorsement of collective Jenna-management is the exactly right note to end on — it's wise, resigned, and says everything about what TGS is like to work at.

tmdb_overview: After being pressured by Jack to plug GE products into her show, Liz integrates Jack into a sketch. While Jack hones his questionable acting chops, Frank and Toofer trick Jenna into fearing for her job and Liz wonders if Tracy is faking illiteracy to skip out on rehearsals.
insight: Early Season 30 Rock hits stride with 67 jokes across 23 minutes — 2.44-per-minute density fuels its 83.5
